name: Cefalexin
route_note: Oral capsules, tablets or suspension, usually 2–4 times daily.

discovery.note: Derived from 7-aminocephalosporanic acid, itself obtained from cephalosporin C produced by Acremonium (Cephalosporium) fungi.

tagline: Oral first-generation cephalosporin for skin, bone and urinary infections
summary: Cefalexin is an orally absorbed first-generation cephalosporin introduced by Eli Lilly in the late 1960s. It is active mainly against streptococci, methicillin-susceptible staphylococci and some Enterobacterales, and is widely used for skin and soft-tissue and urinary infections.
mechanism: Cefalexin inhibits the transpeptidase activity of penicillin-binding proteins, preventing peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing bacterial lysis.
Its cephem nucleus is more stable than penicillins to staphylococcal penicillinase, but it is hydrolysed by many Gram-negative beta-lactamases, and it has no activity against MRSA or enterococci.
uses: Uncomplicated urinary tract infections, including in pregnancy

history.title: Cephalosporium discovery
history.detail: Giuseppe Brotzu isolates an antibiotic-producing Cephalosporium (now Acremonium) fungus from seawater near a sewage outfall in Sardinia.

history.title: Cephalosporin C structure
history.detail: Oxford chemists Edward Abraham and Guy Newton determine the structure of cephalosporin C.

history.title: First cephalosporin
history.detail: Eli Lilly launches cefalotin, the first marketed cephalosporin (injectable).

history.title: Introduction
history.detail: Cefalexin is introduced by Eli Lilly (Keflex), one of the first oral cephalosporins.

history.title: WHO AWaRe classification
history.detail: The WHO Essential Medicines List begins grouping antibiotics into Access, Watch and Reserve categories; cefalexin is placed in the Access group.

facts: Cefalexin is classified in the WHO 'Access' antibiotic group.
Cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy is low overall but higher for cephalosporins with similar side chains, such as cefalexin and ampicillin.
